algorithm.Title: Abdominal Pain - Male
Definition: Pain or discomfort located between the bottom of the rib cage and the groin crease.

PainSeverity.text: Doesn't interfere with normal activities, abdomen soft and not tender to touch.
Interferes with normal activities or awakens from sleep, abdomen tender to touch.
Excruciating pain, doubled over, unable to do any normal activities.

KeyPoints: Abdominal pain is a very common symptom.

Sometimes it may be a symptom of a benign gastrointestinal disorder like gas, overeating, or gastroenteritis. At times abdominal pain is a symptom of a moderately serious problem like appendicitis or biliary colic (gallstones). Abdominal pain may also be the warning symptom of life-threatening conditions like perforated peptic ulcer disease, mesenteric ischemia, and ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Rarely people may have upper abdominal pain as the sole symptom of a heart attack.
Pain in older adults (e.g., over 60 years) carries with it a higher risk of serious illness. In one study of older patients presenting to an E.D. with abdominal pain, 40% had surgical illness.

LocationTable.source: Heart, stomach, duodenum, esophagus, gallbladder, pancreas

Background.ExpertReviewer: Kenneth Lee, MD, Clinical Instructor and Emergency Physician, Emergency Medicine, Northwestern Memorial Hospital Emergency Department, Chicago, IL

FirstAid: FIRST AID Advice for Shock: Lie down with the feet elevated.

advice.Title: Guideline Attribution
Content: Care Advice given per Abdominal Pain - Male (Adult) guideline.

advice.Title: Call Back If
Content: Severe pain lasts over 1 hour
Constant pain lasts over 2 hours
Intermittent pain (comes and goes, cramps) lasts over 48 hours
Increased rectal bleeding
No bowel movement for over 4 days
You become worse

advice.Title: Call Back If
Content: Severe pain lasts over 1 hour
Constant pain lasts over 2 hours
Vomiting or intermittent pain (comes and goes, cramps) lasts over 48 hours
Vomiting blood happens again
Signs of dehydration occur (such as no urine over 12 hours, very dry mouth, lightheaded)
You become worse

advice.Title: Reassurance and Education — Mild Stomachache
Content: It doesn't sound like a serious stomachache. So far it has lasted less than 2 hours.
A stomachache can be from indigestion, gas pains or overeating.
Sometimes a stomachache signals the onset of a vomiting or diarrhea illness from a viral gastroenteritis ("stomach flu").
Here is some care advice that should help.

advice.Title: Reassurance and Education — Short Term Pain
Content: So far this severe pain has lasted less than 1 hour.
Pain that lasts just a short period of time is often not serious.
A stomachache can be from indigestion, gas pains or overeating. Sometimes a stomachache signals the onset of a vomiting or diarrhea illness from a viral gastroenteritis ("stomach flu").
Here is some care advice that should help.

advice.Title: Call EMS 911 Now
Content: Immediate medical attention is needed. You need to hang up and call 911 (or an ambulance).
Triager Discretion: I'll call you back in a few minutes to be sure you were able to reach them.

advice.Title: Go to ED Now
Content: You need to be seen in the Emergency Department.
Go to the ED at ___________ Hospital.
Leave now. Drive carefully.

advice.Title: Go to ED/UCC Now (or PCP Triage)
Content: If No PCP Second-Level Triage: You need to be seen within the next hour. Go to the ED/UCC at _____________ Hospital. Leave as soon as you can. Caution: see Sources of Care.

If PCP Second-Level Triage Required: You may need to be seen. Your doctor (or NP/PA) will want to talk with you. I'll page the provider on-call now. If you haven't heard within 30 minutes, go directly to the ED/UCC.
Note to Triager: Use nurse judgment to select the most appropriate source of care. Do not send these patients to Retail Clinics.
Sources of Care — ED: may need surgery/hospitalization/unstable. UCC Is Open: stable, less serious symptoms (confirm capabilities). Office Is Open: stable and not seriously ill, consult PCP.

advice.Title: See HCP (or PCP Triage) Within 4 Hours
Content: If Office Will Be Open: seen within 3-4 hours; call doctor now or when office opens.
If Office Will Be Closed and No PCP Second-Level Triage: seen within 3-4 hours; a nearby UCC is often a good source of care, or go to the ED. Go sooner if worse.
If Office Will Be Closed and PCP Second-Level Triage Required: doctor will want to talk with you; I'll page on-call now. If on-call provider can't be reached, send to UCC or ED.
Note to Triager: use nurse judgment; consider urgency AND resources needed.

advice.Title: See PCP Within 24 Hours
Content: If Office Will Be Open: examined within 24 hours; call and make an appointment.
If Office Will Be Closed: seen within 24 hours; a clinic or UCC is a good source of care.
If Patient Has No PCP: refer to a clinic or UCC; help caller find a PCP for future care.

advice.Title: See PCP Within 3 Days
Content: You need to be seen within 2 or 3 days.
PCP Visit: call during regular office hours; a clinic/UCC is fine if office is closed. If office opens tomorrow, call then, not in 3 days.
If Patient Has No PCP: a clinic or UCC is fine; help caller find a PCP for future care.

advice.Title: See PCP Within 2 Weeks
Content: You need to be seen for this ongoing problem within the next 2 weeks.
PCP Visit: call during regular office hours and make an appointment.
If Patient Has No PCP: a primary care clinic is where you need to be seen for chronic problems.

advice.Title: Home Care — Information or Advice Only Call
Home Care
Content: You should be able to treat this at home.

advice.Title: Call PCP Now
Content: You need to discuss this with your doctor (or NP/PA).
I'll page the on-call provider now. If you haven't heard within 30 minutes, call again.

advice.Title: Call PCP Within 24 Hours
Content: You need to discuss this with your doctor within the next 24 hours.
If Office Will Be Open: call when it opens tomorrow morning.
If Office Will Be Closed: I'll page the on-call provider now, except 9pm-9am since this isn't urgent.

advice.Title: Call PCP When Office Is Open
Content: You need to discuss this with your doctor within the next few days.
Call the office when it is open.

advice.Title: Go to L&D Now
Content: You need to be seen.
Go to the Labor and Delivery Unit or the Emergency Department.
Leave now. Drive carefully.

advice.Title: Urgent Home Treatment With Follow-Up Call
Content: Call-back instructions.
Call Center Provides RN Call-Backs: you should usually improve with home treatment; I'll call back in 30-60 minutes; call immediately if worse before then.
Call Center Does Not Provide RN Call-Backs: after treatment, call back in 30-60 minutes and tell me how you are doing; if worse or not improved, go to the ED without calling back.
RN Response to Follow-Up Call: if unchanged/worse, refer to ED Now; if improved, review remaining questions and give care advice.

advice.Title: Another Adult Should Drive
Content: It is better and safer if another adult drives instead of you.

advice.Title: Bring Medicines
Content: Bring a list of your current medicines when you go to the Emergency Department.
Bring the pill bottles too, to help confirm the right medicines and dose.

advice.Title: Note to Triager — Ambulance Transport for Bedridden Patient
Content: Because of bedridden state, the patient will likely need ambulance transport and ED exam.
Caregivers can arrange transport via private ambulance company or via EMS 911.

advice.Title: Nothing by Mouth (Possible Surgery)
Content: Do not eat or drink anything for now.
Reason: Condition may need surgery and general anesthesia.

advice.Title: Nothing by Mouth
Content: Do not eat or drink anything for now.

advice.Title: Call Back If Worse
Content: You become worse

advice.Title: Note to Triager — Driving
Content: Another adult should drive.
Patient should not delay going to the emergency department.
If immediate transportation isn't available via car, rideshare, or taxi, instruct patient to call EMS-911.

advice.Title: First Aid — Lie Down for Shock
Content: Lie down with the feet elevated.
Reason: Treatment for shock.

advice.Title: Expected Course — Abdomen Pain
Content: With harmless causes, the pain is usually better or goes away within 2 hours.
With viral gastroenteritis, belly cramps may occur before vomiting/diarrhea bouts and may last 2-3 days.
With serious causes (such as appendicitis) the pain becomes constant and more severe.

advice.Title: Pass a Stool
Content: Sit on the toilet and try to pass a stool.
This may relieve pain if due to constipation, gas, or impending diarrhea.

advice.Title: Reassurance and Education — Stomach Pain
Content: It doesn't sound like a serious stomachache.
A mild stomachache can be from indigestion, stomach irritation, or overeating.
Sometimes a stomachache signals the onset of a vomiting illness from a virus.
Here is some care advice that should help.

advice.Title: Drink Clear Fluids
Content: Drink clear fluids only (water, flat soft drinks, half-strength Gatorade).
Sip small amounts until you feel better and the pain is gone.
Then slowly return to a regular diet.

advice.Title: Avoid Aspirin and NSAIDs
Content: Avoid aspirin and anti-inflammatory medicines (ibuprofen/Motrin, naproxen/Aleve) unless told to by a doctor.
These drugs can irritate the stomach lining and make pain worse.
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) does not cause stomach irritation.

advice.Title: Pain Diary
Content: Keep a pain diary.
Write down date, time, place, activity, severity, duration, what helps.
Reason: Try to find the cause or triggers.

advice.Title: Bring a Sample
Content: Bring in a sample of anything that looks like blood.
Use a plastic bag or container.
Reason: The doctor may want to test it.

advice.Title: Drink Adequate Liquids
Content: Adequate liquid intake keeps bowel movements soft.
Drink 6 to 8 cups (1,500-2,000 ml) of water each day.
Caution: some medical conditions require fluid restriction.
Prune juice is a natural laxative. Avoid alcohol.

advice.Title: General Constipation Instructions
Content: Eat a high fiber diet.
Drink enough liquids.
Exercise regularly — even a daily 15 minute walk helps.
Get into a rhythm; try a BM at the same time each day.
Don't ignore your body's signals. Avoid enemas and stimulant laxatives.

advice.Title: Bring a Bucket in Case of Vomiting
Content: You may wish to bring a bucket, pan, or plastic bag in case of more vomiting during the drive.

advice.Title: High Fiber Diet
Content: A high fiber diet improves intestinal function and softens bowel movements.
Eat fruit and vegetables at each meal (peas, prunes, citrus, apples, beans, corn).
Eat more whole-grain foods (bran flakes, bran muffins, oatmeal, brown rice, whole wheat bread).

advice.Title: Fever Medicine — Acetaminophen
Content: Fever above 101° F (38.3° C) should be treated with acetaminophen (Tylenol).
Goal is to bring fever down to a comfortable level; medicine usually lowers fever 2-3° F (1-1.5° C).
Regular Strength Tylenol: 650 mg (two 325 mg pills) every 4-6 hours as needed; max 10 pills/day (3,250 mg).
Extra Strength Tylenol: 1,000 mg (two 500 mg pills) every 6-8 hours as needed; max 6 pills/day (3,000 mg).
Use the lowest amount of medicine that makes the fever better.

advice.Title: Fever Medicine — Acetaminophen — Extra Notes and Warnings
Content: Follow these dosing instructions unless your doctor told you otherwise.
Acetaminophen is in many OTC and prescription medicines — don't double up. Overdose can hurt the liver.
Caution: do not take acetaminophen if you have liver disease.
Read all package instructions before taking any medicine.

advice.Title: Rest (Until Better)
Content: Lie down.
Rest until you feel better.

advice.Title: Rest (Until Seen)
Content: Lie down.
Rest until you are seen.

advice.Title: Diet — Advance Slowly
Content: Slowly advance diet from clear liquids to a bland diet.
Avoid alcohol or caffeinated beverages.
Avoid greasy or fatty foods.

advice.Title: Diet — Bland
Content: Drink adequate fluids. Eat a bland diet.
Avoid alcohol or caffeinated beverages.
Avoid greasy or fatty foods.

advice.Title: Reassurance — Chronic Stomach Pains Lasting More Than 4 Weeks
Content: See your doctor if you are having long-term problems with stomach pains. Get a check-up.
Here is some care advice that should help.

advice.Title: Bismuth Subsalicylate (Such as Pepto-Bismol)
Content: Helps reduce diarrhea, vomiting, and abdomen cramping. Available OTC.
Adult dosage: two tablets or tablespoons by mouth every hour (if diarrhea continues), max 8 doses/24 hours.
Do not use for more than 2 days.

advice.Title: Bismuth Subsalicylate — Extra Notes and Warnings
Content: May cause temporary darkening of stool and tongue.
Do not use if allergic to aspirin. Do not use in pregnancy.
Talk to your doctor first if you take a blood thinner, have bleeding problems, gout, or kidney disease.
Available under other brand names (e.g., Kaopectate) — follow package dosing, it varies by brand.

advice.Title: Stomach Cramps
Content: Cramps may be due to an intestinal virus or something you ate.
When you have cramps, drink some water, then lie down and find a comfortable position.

advice.Title: Call Back If
Content: Severe pain lasts over 1 hour
Constant pain lasts over 2 hours
You become worse

advice.Title: Call Back If
Content: Severe pain lasts over 1 hour
Constant pain lasts over 2 hours
Moderate pains come and go for more than 24 hours
Mild pains come and go for more than 48 hours
You become worse

advice.Title: Call Back If
Content: Severe pain lasts over 1 hour
Constant pain lasts over 2 hours
Fever occurs
You become worse

advice.Title: Avoid Non-Essential Medicines
Content: Stop all vitamins and non-prescription medicines for 24 hours — may make vomiting worse.
Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen/Advil/Motrin, naproxen/Aleve) — can cause stomach irritation.
Call if vomiting a prescription medicine.

advice.Title: Reassurance — Blood Streaks in Vomit
Content: Hard vomiting can cause a small tear in the lower esophagus lining, healing in under a day.
Our main goal is to bring the vomiting under control.
Here is some care advice that should help.

advice.Title: Retching
Content: For ongoing vomiting (retching), rest the stomach fully for 2 hours.
After 2 hours, start with small amounts of clear fluids.

initialAssessmentQuestions._note: Sourced from Algorithm.Definition free-text history questions, not from the Question (TAQ) table.
initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: "Where does it hurt?" — click the body map
"When did the pain begin?"
Prompts: Examples: minutes, hours or days ago

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: "Does the pain come and go, or is it constant?"
Prompts: If it comes and goes: "How long does it last?" "Do you have pain now?"
Note: Comes and goes means the pain is intermittent. It goes away completely between bouts.
If constant: "Is it getting better, staying the same, or getting worse?"
Note: Constant means the pain never goes away completely; most serious pain is constant and gets worse.
initialAssessmentQuestions.Placeholder: If intermittent: how long does each bout last? Pain now?

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: "How bad is the pain?" (Scale 1–10)
Prompts: MILD (1–3): Doesn't interfere with normal activities, abdomen soft and not tender to touch.
MODERATE (4–7): Interferes with normal activities or awakens from sleep, abdomen tender to touch.
SEVERE (8–10): Excruciating pain, doubled over, unable to do any normal activities.

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: "Have you ever had this type of stomach pain before?"
Prompts: If Yes, ask: "When was the last time?" and "What happened that time?"
initialAssessmentQuestions.Placeholder: If yes: when was the last time? What happened?

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: "What do you think is causing the stomach pain?"
"What makes it better or worse?"
Prompts: Examples: antacids, bending or twisting motion, bowel movement
initialAssessmentQuestions.Placeholder: e.g., antacids help; worse with movement...

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: "Do you have any other symptoms?"
Prompts: Examples: back pain, diarrhea, fever, urination pain, vomiting
